title: The British Flag Theorem
description: For any point P in the plane of a rectangle ABCD, the sums of squared distances to opposite corners are equal: PA² + PC² = PB² + PD².

meta.author: Classical (formalized in Lean 4)
originalContributions: Coordinate formalization of the British Flag theorem (absent from Mathlib and the existing gallery)
Rectangle encoded by two algebraic conditions: a parallelogram closure C = B + D − A and a right angle at A expressed as orthogonality of the edge vectors
Single-step proof: the difference (PA² + PC²) − (PB² + PD²) equals twice the dot product of the edge vectors, which vanishes by the right-angle hypothesis (`linear_combination`)
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The rectangle is encoded by the parallelogram closure C = B + D − A and the orthogonality of edges B − A and D − A.

overview.historicalContext: The British Flag theorem is a classical result of elementary Euclidean geometry. Its name comes from the picture that results when the four squared-distance segments from an interior point are drawn to the corners of a rectangle: the diagonals and the connecting lines sketch a pattern resembling the Union Jack. Despite its elementary statement it is a recurring exercise in coordinate geometry and a clean illustration of how an orthogonality condition controls a metric identity.
overview.problemStatement:
**British Flag Theorem**: Let ABCD be a rectangle and P any point in its plane (A and C are opposite corners, as are B and D). Then

PA² + PC² = PB² + PD².
overview.text: For any point and any rectangle, the sums of squared distances to the two pairs of opposite corners are equal.
overview.proofStrategy:
We work in the coordinate plane ℝ × ℝ and use the squared-distance function sqDist P Q = (P.1 − Q.1)² + (P.2 − Q.2)². A rectangle is encoded by two conditions on its vertices: a parallelogram closure C = B + D − A (so the figure closes up), and a right angle at A, written as the orthogonality (B.1 − A.1)(D.1 − A.1) + (B.2 − A.2)(D.2 − A.2) = 0.

Writing u = B − A and v = D − A, expanding the four squared distances gives

(PA² + PC²) − (PB² + PD²) = 2 (u.1 · v.1 + u.2 · v.2) = 2 (u ⬝ v).

This is exactly twice the orthogonality form, so it vanishes precisely because of the right-angle hypothesis. After substituting the parallelogram closure the identity is closed by a single `linear_combination` step against the orthogonality hypothesis.
keyInsights: The British Flag theorem is the orthogonality condition in disguise: the metric identity holds exactly when the edge vectors at A are perpendicular
Encoding 'rectangle' as parallelogram-closure plus a single right angle is enough — the remaining three right angles follow and are not needed for the identity
The whole content reduces to one algebraic fact: (PA² + PC²) − (PB² + PD²) = 2 (u ⬝ v), where u, v are the edge vectors at A
Because the identity is an exact cancellation, the proof needs no square roots and no irrational arithmetic — it is a single ring/linear_combination identity over ℝ
prerequisites: Coordinate geometry of points in the plane
Squared Euclidean distance and the dot product
The notion that a right angle is the vanishing of a dot product

mainTheorems.name: british_flag
mainTheorems.description: For a rectangle A B C D (parallelogram closure C = B + D − A with a right angle at A) and any point P, PA² + PC² = PB² + PD².
mainTheorems.leanType: C = (B.1 + D.1 − A.1, B.2 + D.2 − A.2) → (B.1 − A.1)·(D.1 − A.1) + (B.2 − A.2)·(D.2 − A.2) = 0 → sqDist P A + sqDist P C = sqDist P B + sqDist P D

sections.title: Coordinate Setup and Squared Distance
sections.summary: Model planar points as ℝ × ℝ and define sqDist P Q = (P.1 − Q.1)² + (P.2 − Q.2)².
sections.mathContext: The squared Euclidean distance between $(p_1,p_2)$ and $(q_1,q_2)$ is $(p_1-q_1)^2 + (p_2-q_2)^2$. Using squared distance avoids square roots entirely, since the theorem is an identity among squared lengths.

sections.title: The British Flag Identity
sections.summary: Substitute the parallelogram closure and reduce the goal to twice the orthogonality form, discharged by linear_combination.
sections.mathContext: With $u = B - A$, $v = D - A$, expansion gives $(PA^2 + PC^2) - (PB^2 + PD^2) = 2(u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2)$, which is zero by the right-angle hypothesis $u \cdot v = 0$.

crossReferences.description: The British Flag theorem generalizes the Pythagorean relation; when P is a corner it reduces to the Pythagorean identity on the rectangle's sides and diagonal
Both results expand squared distances via the dot product; the British Flag theorem is the special case where the relevant angle is a right angle, so the cosine term 2(u·v) vanishes

Another classical identity relating distances among the vertices of a cyclic quadrilateral; like the British Flag theorem it constrains the four corner-to-point distances, but multiplicatively rather than as a sum of squares

conclusion.summary: The British Flag theorem is formalized by a direct coordinate computation. Encoding the rectangle by a parallelogram closure and a single right angle, the difference of the two squared-distance sums collapses to twice the dot product of the edge vectors, which vanishes by orthogonality. The formalization is fully verified — 0 axioms, 0 sorries — and self-contained over Mathlib.
conclusion.implications: The identity exposes the British Flag theorem as a metric restatement of perpendicularity. The same coordinate method handles the higher-dimensional analogue (a box in ℝⁿ) and the converse direction, where the equality of squared-distance sums forces the right angle.
openQuestions: Does the squared-distance equality PA² + PC² = PB² + PD² for all P characterize rectangles among parallelograms?
What is the sharp n-dimensional generalization for a rectangular box and its space diagonal corners?
